{{DISPLAYTITLE:''Synopsis of Pure Mathematics''}}
'''''Synopsis of Pure Mathematics'''''<ref>The full title is, "A synopsis of elementary results in pure mathematics: containing propositions, formulæ, and methods of analysis, with abridged demonstrations. Supplemented by an index to the papers on pure mathematics which are to be found in the principal journals and transactions of learned societies, both English and foreign, of the present century"</ref> is a book by [[G. S. Carr]], written in 1886.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Review of ''A Synopsis of Elementary Results in Pure Mathematics'' by G. S. Carr|journal=Science|date=25 May 1888|volume=XI|issue=277|page=251|url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uc1.31822020652350;view=1up;seq=273}}</ref> The book attempted to summarize the state of most of the basic mathematics known at the time.

The book is noteworthy because it was a major source of information for the legendary and self-taught mathematician [[Srinivasa Ramanujan]] who managed to obtain a library loaned copy from a friend in 1903.<ref>''A to Z of mathematicians'' by Tucker McElroy 2005 {{isbn|0-8160-5338-3}} page 221</ref> Ramanujan reportedly studied the contents of the book in detail.<ref name=papers /> The book is generally acknowledged as a key element in awakening the genius of Ramanujan.<ref name=papers >''Collected papers of Srinivasa Ramanujan'' Srinivasa Ramanujan Aiyangar, Godfrey Harold Hardy, P. Veṅkatesvara Seshu Aiyar 2000 {{isbn|0-8218-2076-1}} page xii</ref>

Carr acknowledged the main sources of his book in its preface:

{{blockquote|... In the Algebra, Theory of Equations, and Trigonometry sections, I am largely indebted to [[Isaac Todhunter|Todhunter]]'s well-known treatises ...

In the section entitled Elementary Geometry, I have added to simpler propositions a selection of theorems from Townsend's Modern Geometry and [[George Salmon|Salmon]]'s Conic Sections.

In Geometric Conics, the line of demonstration followed agrees, in the main, with that adopted in Drew's treatise on the subject. ...

The account of the C. G. S. system given in the preliminary section, has been compiled from a valuable contribution on the subject by [[Joseph David Everett|Professor Everett]], of Belfast, published by the Physical Society of London.

In addition to the authors already named, the following treatises have been consulted—Algebras, by Wood, Bourdon, and Lefebvre de Fourey; Snowball's Trigonometry; Salmon's Higher Algebra; the geometrical exercises in Pott's Euclid; and Geometrical Conics by Taylor, Jackson, and Renshaw.<ref>{{cite book|author=Carr, G. S.|title=A synopsis of elementary results in pure mathematics|location=London|publisher=F. Hodgson|year=1886|pages=vi–ix|url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uc1.b4506135;view=1up;seq=12}}</ref>}}
